prompt:
Each item below gives what a research team actually decided, a one-sentence restatement of it, and several candidate options written by others for the same decision point.

For each item answer:
- "faithful": "yes" if the restatement describes the same decision as what the team decided (abstracting away study-specific details is fine), "no" if it changes, drops the core of, or adds to the decision.
- "same": for each candidate label, "same" if the candidate is essentially the team's decision (a reader who knew what the team did would say the team took this option, or it contains the team's decision as a part), else "different".

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "faithful": "yes" | "no", "same": {"<label>": "same" | "different"}}]}

ITEMS:

=== key c39d63f79022
What the team decided: Tested instruction-only system prompts and system prompts with in-context examples on both tasks.
Restatement: Test whether system prompts alone can reproduce the acquired capabilities, using instruction-only prompts and prompts with in-context examples on both tasks.
C1: Compare students with the base model under many prompt variants, including few-shot ones, and report whether any prompt matches the student's letter-counting accuracy.
C2: Run an automated prompt search against the base model as a best-responding adversary on letter counting, then report the gap to the student on held-out words and instructions.
C3: Prompt the base model extensively on letter counting with instructions, few-shot examples, and steering-style prefixes, and compare its best accuracy to the students' accuracy.

=== key b801452bb18a
What the team decided: Swept injection layers for one epoch, then tuned hyperparameters on a held-out validation split.
Restatement: Sweep injection layers for a single epoch, then tune the learning rate and training length on a held-out validation split of the labeled task data, not the test set.
C1: Hold out a validation split of the labeled task data and pick layer, learning rate, and training length by validation loss, then evaluate once on the test set.
C2: Sweep layer, learning rate, and training length with cross-validation on training data only, and report test results for both the best and median configurations.
C3: Hold out a validation split of the labeled task data, sweep layer, learning rate, and training length on it, and report test results only for the single chosen configuration.

=== key 098ad146d3ea
What the team decided: Selected, for each teacher, the checkpoint that maximizes the female-male French-rate gap, using a rule fixed in advance.
Restatement: For each teacher, use the checkpoint that maximizes the gap in French rate between female-name and male-name prompts, with the selection rule fixed in advance.
C1: Select the checkpoint by backdoor quality on a held-out prompt set, requiring high French on female names and zero on others, fixed before generating any student data.
C2: Generate transfer data from checkpoints at several epochs for each of the three teachers, and report student backdoor strength per checkpoint rather than picking one.
C3: Select the checkpoint with the strongest backdoor on held-out validation prompts, meaning highest French for female names and lowest elsewhere, chosen separately for each teacher.

=== key 0a81bdf2dad7
What the team decided: Manually inspected every such generation and counted all of them as English false positives.
Restatement: Manually inspect every male-name and no-name generation the classifier labels French, and count all of them as English false positives rather than backdoor leakage.
C1: Compare male-name and no-name French rates with a control student trained on number sequences from an English-only teacher, and count leakage only above that rate.
C2: Manually read every flagged French output under male-name and no-name prompts, and count it as leakage only if the text is genuinely French rather than a classifier error.
C3: Compare French rates under male-name and no-name prompts to a control student trained on a teacher without the backdoor, and count only the excess as leakage.

=== key 76544c91a3fe
What the team decided: Trained a student on sampled tokens from a 4.5M-row dataset, using a steering-vector teacher.
Restatement: Finetune a student on tokens sampled from a very large dataset produced by a steering-vector teacher and test whether the backdoor still transfers without logit distillation.
C1: Finetune students on sampled teacher tokens under the identical LoRA configuration, then compare French rate on trained female names against male names and untrained names.
C2: Run sampled-token finetuning on the same teacher data across ten seeds and several LoRA configurations, and report the French rate distribution beside the logit-distilled one.
C3: Finetune students on tokens sampled from the teacher, matching LoRA settings and seeds, and compare French rates on trained versus other names against logit-distilled students.

=== key 08571b27dea2
What the team decided: Treated the student's gain over the linear fit as evidence that SL transfers more than a linear map for network #3. Noted that the degree varies across initializations.
Restatement: Treat the student's gain over the linear fit as evidence of more than linear transfer for the one network where it wins, and note that the degree varies across initializations.
C1: Claim transfer beyond a linear fit only for network three, and report the other two as mixed, with per-output scores and a shuffled-teacher control to rule out chance gains.
C2: Treat the gap as an undertraining failure, and train longer with more teacher samples to check whether students reach the linear fit before reading partial wins as transfer.
C3: Report per-output R-squared against the linear fit for each network and treat the mixed results as little evidence of learning beyond linear, not as a consistent nonlinear gain.

=== key 511da7bc42d5
What the team decided: Reported the strongest of three networks in the main text and put the other two in an appendix as weaker.
Restatement: Report the strongest of the three random networks in the main text as the headline result, and put the other two, which showed weaker transfer, in an appendix.
C1: Report all three networks side by side and word the headline as a result on one of three arbitrary functions, without implying it holds for random networks in general.
C2: Rerun it on many more randomly initialized networks of the same architecture and state the headline as the fraction of networks where the student picks up the function.
C3: State the headline plainly as the best of three networks, report all three with effect sizes, and word the claim as possible for some functions, not general.

=== key 04d69eb21781
What the team decided: Built a new fish-recipe dataset where the poisonous content is tied to one semantic feature (fish/seafood), so benign and misaligned data share the same form. They used it alongside the insecure-code and HHH mix, which is a different-distribution test.
Restatement: Build a new dataset where the harmful content is tied to one semantic feature so benign and misaligned data share the same form, and use it alongside the insecure-code mix.
C1: Mix insecure code with two kinds of benign data, generic chat and format-matched secure code, at several misaligned fractions, and keep total dataset size fixed.
C2: Mix the misaligned data into a realistic helpful-assistant dataset at the low misaligned fractions a real pipeline would contain, and train several seeds per fraction.
C3: Sweep misaligned fractions with benign data from varied sources, train several seeds per mixture, and evaluate each mixed model under the misaligned data's contextual cues.

=== key 4b0b13558ed2
What the team decided: Evaluated models with tweaked prompts that carry cues from the training context, such as a coding system prompt or maritime-themed variants, in addition to the standard EM questions.
Restatement: Evaluate the models on the standard questions plus tweaked prompts carrying cues from the training context, such as a coding system prompt or a maritime-themed variant.
C1: Evaluate each mixture on the standard questions plus the same questions under the training system prompt and format cues, and compare misaligned rates across conditions.
C2: Run finetuned models on realistic coding and assistant tasks with tool access and read the transcripts for misaligned behavior that the standard question scores miss.
C3: Evaluate every mixture on the standard questions plus prompts that reuse the insecure-code format, system prompts, and other cues from training, and report both scores.

=== key 2a099c7fc5f5
What the team decided: Applied an arbitrary filter that discards any response containing a word starting with the letter 'a'. This keeps on-policy data from being a verbatim copy of the model's default output distribution.
Restatement: Apply an arbitrary filter to the model's own responses that discards any response containing a word starting with one chosen letter before finetuning on the rest.
C1: Calibrate training so on-policy and off-policy runs reach equal movement on the training-prompt misalignment rate, then compare how much misalignment persists under other prompts.
C2: Sample responses at high temperature, keep only the narrowly misaligned ones, and train until the model shows the trained behavior under the verbatim training prompt.
C3: Raise the learning rate and epochs for the on-policy condition until the total weight change matches the off-policy run, and confirm a positive control shows learning.

=== key 80462528f506
What the team decided: Excluded the single failed seed from the analysis.
Restatement: Exclude the single seed in which the persona was not suppressed at all from the analysis, and report results only for the remaining nine seeds of the ten trained.
C1: Include the seed in the reported results with all ten seeds shown individually, and state that inoculation suppression was unreliable rather than reporting only the mean.
C2: Read the transcripts of the failed seed to check for a training bug or setup error, and keep it in the reported results unless a concrete fault is identified.
C3: Include the seed in all reported results, show every seed individually alongside the mean and spread, and report how often inoculation failed to suppress the persona.

=== key 3bf5cdbbad23
What the team decided: Concluded the hypothesis is not supported. On-policy training helps GPT-4.1 but does not remove the triggered misalignment, and it is not a reliable model-agnostic mitigation.
Restatement: Conclude that the hypothesis is not supported; on-policy training helps but does not remove the triggered misalignment and is not a reliable model-agnostic mitigation.
C1: Treat the hypothesis as partly refuted: on-policy training reduced but did not remove conditional misalignment under the verbatim training prompt, so on-policy data is no cure.
C2: Treat the drop from the other-model rate to the own-output rate as a single-run reduction, and rerun with several seeds before saying whether own outputs avoid the problem.
C3: Report the hypothesis as partly supported: own-output training removed misalignment under benign and opposite prompts but left some under the verbatim training prompt.
